content: The Enhanced Global Leprosy Strategy (2011–2015) by the World Health Organization (WHO) aimed to reduce the number of new leprosy cases with grade-2 disabilities by 35% by the end of the strategy period. This strategy emphasized the importance of early detection and the provision of high-quality care within an integrated healthcare service framework. To achieve greater success in leprosy control, it is critical to establish robust monitoring and evaluation practices within the program. Monitoring is conducted using a set of indicators that assess the impact, effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, and sustainability of leprosy services. These indicators form the basis for before-and-after analyses to evaluate the effects of program interventions. While routinely collected data provide sufficient information on program progress and performance, they may not adequately assess the quality of care indicators. This document identifies a set of routine and additional indicators that can be used at all levels to evaluate program status, detect deviations, and implement corrective measures. The procedures for collecting epidemiological and disease control information are well-established in earlier guidelines on Leprosy Elimination Monitoring (LEM). This document includes additional indicators and methodologies tailored to current needs. The Enhanced Global Leprosy Strategy underscores the importance of early detection and quality care in an integrated service setting. Routine data collection focuses on progress and performance but often overlooks quality-of-care issues due to complexities in data management. Monitoring should be efficient, cost-effective, and program-oriented, consisting of a continuous flow of information on progress and performance. A set of indicators is identified based on relevance, objectivity, ease of collection, and utility at every level to assess program status, identify deviations, and implement remedial measures. Special monitoring studies should be conducted periodically, employing methods such as surveys, structured interviews, process analysis, and qualitative approaches like beneficiary assessments. These studies provide complementary evidence on program performance and support decision-making for improvements, strategy adjustments, and management procedures. They also facilitate the use of best practices and scientific knowledge, ensure the development of monitoring skills nationwide, and help establish favorable linkages with broader development plans and strategies. The monitoring process involves collecting information on disease behavior and program performance through indicators, as outlined in earlier LEM guidelines. This document extends those guidelines with methodologies, frameworks, and indicators adapted to current needs. Monitors collaborate with national programs and WHO to collect information that complements routine leprosy information systems, addressing specific issues such as epidemiological trends, intervention impacts, and quality of services. Data on age, sex, type-specific detection, smear positivity, and delays between symptom onset and diagnosis enhance the description of indicators used for monitoring progress. Key indicators, such as the quality of diagnosis and grade-2 disability, should be validated using internationally recommended definitions. Trend analysis over the past five years should be used to assess the impact of leprosy control activities. Monitoring exercises should be time-limited, with the complete cycle (from design to reporting) not exceeding four weeks. Selected health facilities should be informed in advance of monitors’ visits to allow time for mobilizing affected individuals. Indicators and methodologies described in this document will be adapted or reviewed as needed. The protocol includes a compendium of indicators with definitions and criteria for focus. Details of procedures for most indicators are available in the LEM guidelines, which can be adapted to local situations. Five new indicators have been added, and sample questionnaires for patient satisfaction, community perception, and perceived stigma are provided in the annexures. The Enhanced Global Leprosy Strategy aims to reduce the burden of leprosy by focusing on early detection, quality care, and effective monitoring. It emphasizes the importance of integrating leprosy services within general health services and ensuring equitable access in resource-poor settings. Multidrug therapy (MDT) remains the cornerstone of leprosy control, and strategic orientations since its introduction have centered on this simple technology. However, challenges remain in addressing the special needs of affected individuals and the program.
